reason: The provided sources support 14 multi-site verified claims covering the Apollo 13 oxygen tank explosion, using the lunar module as a lifeboat, and building a makeshift carbon dioxide filter adapter.
story: On April 11, 1970, Apollo 13 launched toward the Moon carrying Jim Lovell, Fred Haise, and Jack Swigert. Nearly 56 hours into the flight, an oxygen tank exploded in the service module, destroying the oxygen supply and cutting off primary electrical power. Stranded 200,000 miles from Earth, the crew was forced to abandon their lunar landing and use the Lunar Module Aquarius as a makeshift lifeboat. Because the lander was built for two people, carbon dioxide quickly built up to dangerous levels. The Command Module had spare filter canisters, but they were the wrong shape. Mission Control engineered a crude adapter using plastic bags, cardstock, spacesuit hoses, and duct tape, radioing instructions up to space. The crew built the contraption, immediately dropping carbon dioxide levels. In freezing cabin temperatures, the astronauts endured the long trip home, splashing down safely in the Pacific Ocean on April 17 before 40 million television viewers.
angle: To prevent suffocation inside a lunar module built for two, Apollo 13 astronauts built a life-saving air filter adapter using plastic covers, cardstock, and duct tape.

claims.claim: Apollo 13 launched on April 11, 1970, intended as NASA's third lunar landing mission.
Jack Swigert replaced Ken Mattingly on the prime crew shortly before launch after Mattingly was exposed to German measles.
An oxygen tank in the service module exploded nearly 56 hours into the flight.
The explosion destroyed the spacecraft's oxygen supply and disabled its electrical power generation.
Swigert and Lovell reported the emergency to Mission Control using the words 'Houston, we've had a problem.'
The three astronauts used the Lunar Module Aquarius as a makeshift lifeboat to survive the journey back to Earth.
The Lunar Module was designed to support only two astronauts, forcing all three crew members to crowd inside.
The Command Module's lithium hydroxide carbon dioxide filter canisters were incompatible in shape with the Lunar Module's filter slots.
Engineers on the ground designed a makeshift filter adapter using plastic covers or bags, cardstock, and duct tape.
Building the improvised carbon dioxide filter allowed carbon dioxide levels inside the Lunar Module to drop immediately.
Powering down nonessential systems to conserve energy caused temperatures inside the spacecraft cabin to drop close to freezing.
Lunar Module pilot Fred Haise developed an infection during the cold return trip.
All three astronauts returned safely to Earth, splashing down in the South Pacific Ocean on April 17, 1970.
An estimated 40 million Americans and tens of millions worldwide watched the live television broadcast of the splashdown.

disputed: Use of a sock in the filter: Prompts or legends mention a sock, but NASA sources specify plastic covers, cardstock, spacesuit hoses, and duct tape. Script should leave out the sock detail.

Famous quote phrasing: Popular media quotes 'Houston, we have a problem', but transcripts show the actual radio message was 'Houston, we've had a problem'. Script should clarify or present the exact historical quote.

Fred Haise's illness detail: Source S1 identifies it as a urinary tract infection, while S3 describes it as a kidney infection. Script should refer to it generally as an infection resulting from severe water rationing.
